issues.legal_issue: A pleading amendment seeking declaratory relief may be allowed despite an alleged limitation bar when the limitation question is genuinely disputed and requires determination at trial.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a pending suit seeking injunction and possession and later sought to add a prayer declaring their ownership.
The defendants disputed the plaintiffs’ title in their written statement.
The defendants contended that the declaration claim was out of time, while the plaintiffs relied on different limitation periods; the applicable limitation period was therefore disputed.
The original plaint already contained factual averments concerning the plaintiffs’ title, and allowing the amendment would permit the limitation question to be tried.
issues.conclusion: The amendment should be allowed, and the trial court should frame and decide the limitation issue in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court has discretion to allow amendments, including when an amended claim may be time-barred, and must exercise that discretion judiciously in the interests of justice. Limitation is a factor in that exercise, not an absolute bar to amendment. Where limitation is disputed and arguable, it may be decided as an issue after amendment. The Court relied on L.J. Leach and Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co. (AIR 1957 SC 357), T.N. Alloy Foundry Co. Ltd. v. T.N. Electricity Board (2004) 3 SCC 392, and Ragu Thilak D. John v. S. Rayappan (2001) 2 SCC 472.

predicates.pending_suit_amendment: A plaintiff sought to amend pleadings in a pending civil suit.
predicates.limitation_disputed: The parties disputed whether the proposed claim was out of time and which limitation period applied.
predicates.amendment_serves_justice: Allowing the amendment would help resolve the dispute in the pending suit and avoid further litigation.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff seeks an amendment in a pending suit, the limitation question is disputed, and allowing the amendment serves justice, the amendment may be allowed while leaving limitation for trial.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for declaratory relief is not necessarily a different relief when the original pleading already sets out the material factual basis for the claimed right.
material_facts: The plaintiffs’ original plaint contained factual averments concerning their title to the property.
The defendants denied that title in their written statement.
The proposed amendment sought a declaration of ownership based on the title facts already pleaded.
issues.conclusion: The proposed declaration was not a different relief that justified refusing the amendment; the disputed title remained to be decided at trial.
issues.legal_principle: The court must assess an amendment in light of the pleaded factual basis and the dispute to be tried. Where the original pleading already sets out the necessary factual basis for the asserted right, a related declaratory prayer does not, merely because it adds a form of relief, introduce a different relief. The Court applied the approach in Ragu Thilak D. John v. S. Rayappan (2001) 2 SCC 472.

predicates.pending_suit_amendment: A plaintiff sought to amend pleadings in a pending civil suit.
predicates.related_declaratory_relief: The plaintiff sought a declaration concerning a right that was the subject of the existing suit.
predicates.title_basis_already_pleaded: The plaintiff had already pleaded the material facts supporting the claimed title or right.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff seeks related declaratory relief in a pending suit and has already pleaded the material facts supporting the right, the amendment is not rejected merely as a different relief.
